title: Born in a grove
hook: on the road to her parents' home, Maya gives birth holding a branch in the Lumbini garden

segments.voice: Yesterday: the white elephant dream, a queen's dream, and a son foretold. Your line was some things announce themselves. What small beginning did you notice? Day twenty-three.
screen: `THE WHITE ELEPHANT DREAM — SOME THINGS ANNOUNCE THEMSELVES.`

segments.voice: Queen Maya is heavily pregnant, and she wants to go home. Not to the palace. To her parents' home, in a town called Devadaha, the way many women of her time went back to their mothers to give birth. So the king has the road smoothed and decorated, and she sets out in a golden palanquin, with a crowd of attendants. Halfway there, the road passes a grove of sal trees in full bloom. Flowers everywhere, bees humming, birds singing. The queen asks to stop. She wants to walk in the garden for a while. She never makes it to her mother's house.
screen: `MAYA WANTS TO GO HOME.` → `A GROVE IN FULL BLOOM.` → `SHE NEVER ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: The grove is called Lumbini. As the story is told, the queen walks to a great sal tree and reaches up for a branch, and the branch bends down to her hand. And standing there, holding the branch, she gives birth. No palace, no bed, no midwives from court. A garden on the way somewhere. The wonders are older still, from the early discourses: the child is received first by gods, two streams of water fall from the sky to wash mother and son, and the baby stands, takes seven steps, looks in every direction, and says this is his last birth. Every Buddhist tradition tells some form of this scene, and in many temples the image of the newborn, one hand pointing up and one down, is bathed with sweet water on his birthday. Now here's the part that isn't legend. A century or two after the Buddha's death, depending on whose dating you follow, the emperor Ashoka, who had become a Buddhist, came to Lumbini on pilgrimage and set up a stone pillar with an inscription. It says, in effect, that here the Buddha, the sage of the Sakyas, was born, and that because of this the village's taxes were lowered. The pillar was lost for centuries, then found again in eighteen ninety-six. It still stands, in southern Nepal. Pilgrims from all over the world walk there. So this is a real place with a real stone. And the story of it is about arriving before you arrive. The most important birth in the tradition didn't happen at home. It happened on the road, under a tree, on the way somewhere else.
screen: `THE BRANCH BENDS TO HER HAND.` · `SEVEN STEPS.` · `ASHOKA'S PILLAR, IN STONE.` · `FOUND AGAIN IN 1896.` · then, large: `BORN ON THE WAY SOMEWHERE.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you two minutes. If you can, go and stand under a tree for one minute of it: in a yard, a street, a park. If you can't, picture one clearly, or look at a plant near you. Feel the ground under your feet. Look up into the branches. Notice how a tree is always in the middle of becoming something: budding, dropping, growing. Then close your eyes, and let the breath be your garden for the rest of the time. The bell holds the time.
Lumbini. The garden where the Buddha was born, on the road between two homes, marked by Ashoka's pillar in southern Nepal.
Your line: born on the way somewhere. Today, notice one good thing that happened to you in between plans: on a detour, a delay, a wrong turn. Day twenty-three.

howItsDone: Buddhists celebrate the Buddha's birth at Vesak, or in East Asia on a birthday festival in spring, often by pouring sweet water or tea over a small statue of the newborn Buddha; Lumbini, in Nepal, is one of the four great pilgrimage places.

fork.setup: you're Queen Maya, on the road to your parents' home. you pass a sal grove in full bloom. what do you do?
options: stop to walk in the garden.
fork.reveal: she stops to walk in the garden, reaches for a sal branch, and gives birth there. the Buddha is born on the way, not at home.

original.note: The name of the garden where the Buddha was born, now in southern Nepal.

trapdoor: what you thought: some place in India.
what it means: the garden in present-day Nepal where Maya gave birth on the road, holding a branch.
what a scholar hears: Ashoka's Rummindei pillar inscription (c. 249 BCE), rediscovered in 1896, names the site as the Buddha's birthplace and records a tax reduction for the village.

sources.ref: Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 123): the birth wonders and the seven steps
Nidanakatha (introduction to the Jataka commentary): the journey to Devadaha and the birth in Lumbini

notes: MN 123 wonders paraphrased: received by devas, two streams of water, seven steps, 'this is my last birth'. Confirm.

Ashoka's pillar: about 250 years after the Buddha (depending on dating), inscription paraphrased (birthplace of the Buddha, the Sakyan sage; village made tax-free except for one-eighth share). Rediscovered 1896. Confirm the paraphrase 'taxes were lowered'.
The branch in the Nidanakatha is of a sal tree; some later tellings name an ashoka tree. Confirm.
Bathing the Buddha is especially East Asian (and Vesak in some countries); confirm howItsDone wording.

Audit (second sample): 'about two hundred and fifty years after the Buddha' did not fit either scholarly chronology for Ashoka's visit (c. 249 BCE); now 'a century or two after the Buddha's death, depending on whose dating you follow'. 'The oldest discourses add wonders' made the canonical MN 123 wonders sound like later additions to the Nidanakatha story; reworded.
